##  Learning Objective

In this lab, you will learn about important aerial photogrammetry parameters:

- **Field of View (FOV)**
- **Ground Sampling Distance (GSD)**
- **Image Overlap**

Understanding these terms will allow you connect image size, image number, image overlap, and flying altitude in planning a field UAV mission.


## Description

When planning fieldwork with a small UAV (sUAV) for Structure from Motion (SfM), key camera and flight parameters must be carefully coordinated. Camera properties like focal length and sensor size determine the field of view (FOV), which in turn influences the ground sampling distance (GSD)—the size of each pixel on the ground and a key measure of image resolution. A smaller GSD (i.e., higher resolution) enables more precise 3D models and measurements but requires flying lower or using higher-quality cameras. Finally, image overlap is critical for SfM, as the software reconstructs 3D structure by matching features across multiple overlapping images. Balancing these factors ensures optimal image quality, coverage, and data accuracy for successful photogrammetric outputs.

Read through the sections in the course book about FOV, GSD, and overlap to get a more solid understanding.

1. **Question 1** Choose two drones from the table above and the following equations to calculate the **Field of View (FOV)** in **degrees** (angular measurement of camera), then convert this FOV to meters on the ground based on the sensor size and focal length for heights of 20, 50, and 100 meters. Your final result will provide the FOV ground size for each UAV above, at the three heights listed, in both horizontal and vertical directions.

For example:

| Drone          | Altitude_m | FOV_degrees_h | FOV_degrees_v | FOV_ground_m_h | FOV_ground_m_h | 
| -------------- | ---------- | ------------- | ------------- | -------------- | -------------- |
| Phantom 4 Pro  | 20 m       |               |               |                |                |
| Phantom 4 Pro  | 50 m       |               |               |                |                |
| Phantom 4 Pro  | 100 m      |               |               |                |                |
| Phantom 4 Pro  | 250 m      |               |               |                |                |
| Mini 4 Pro     | 20 m       |               |               |                |                |

The **FOV** in radians for one dimension (width or height) is calculated by the camera’s sensor size and focal length:

$$
FOV_{\text{radians}} = 2 \times \arctan\left(\frac{\text{Sensor Dimension (mm)}}{2 \times \text{Focal Length (mm)}}\right)
$$
This equation above calculates the angular field of view (in radians) for either the width or height of the camera’s view. Radians can be converted to degrees with $\text{degrees} = \text{radians} \times \frac{180}{\pi}$. To convert the angular FOV into linear distance on the ground, i.e., the width or height of the area visible in one photo, assuming a flat surface and nadir (straight-down) view.

Convert this to **meters on the ground** by multiplying by the flight altitude (H) (in meters):

$$
FOV_{\text{ground}} = 2 \times H \times \tan\left(\frac{FOV_{\text{radians}}}{2}\right)
$$
<br/>

2. **Question 2** Use the FOV and image resolution to estimate **Ground Sampling Distance (GSD)** (the ground area represented by each pixel) for your two drones at each height above ground level in **cm/px**. Only report GSD in the width dimention.

Calculate the GSD for width and height:

$$
GSD_{\text{width}} = \frac{FOV_{\text{ground width}}}{\text{Image_width (in px)}}
$$

*Note:* GSD is in meters per pixel (m/px). Divide by 100 to get cm/px.

5. **Question 5** You are planning a drone flight at 100 meters altitude using the Phantom 4 Pro. If you require 66.7% frontal overlap and the FOV ground height at that altitude is 71.2 meters, how far apart should your images be captured along the flight path?

A few useful equations and some information to help with image overlap include the following:

To capture each pixel in **9 images** (3 × 3 grid), the required overlap percentage is:

$$
\text{Overlap} = \frac{2}{3} = 0.667 = 66.7%
$$

To calculate the spacing between images in meters when accounting for overlap, you can use the general equation:

$$
\text{Spacing (m)} = \text{Image Dimension} \times (1 - \text{Overlap})
$$
The FOV ground height can also be used in this instance. For example:

$$
\text{Spacing (m)} = FOV_{\text{ground height}} \times (1 - Overlap)
$$

The spacing describes either the frontal or lateral distance between flight paths (position at different time) for a UAV.

<br/>

6. **Question 6** You are flying a drone that captures a photo every 2.5 seconds. At 80 meters altitude, the photo height (i.e., vertical ground coverage per image) is 50 meters. To ensure 70% longitudinal overlap, what is the **maximum drone speed** you can fly while still achieving this overlap? Use the equation below.

$$
\text{Longitudinal Overlap (%)} = \left( \frac{\text{Photo Height} - (\text{Speed} \times \text{Photo Interval})}{\text{Photo Height}} \right) \times 100
$$

- *Photo Height* is the vertical coverage of the image on the ground (in meters)
- *Speed* is the ground speed of the drone (in meters per second)
- *Photo Interval* is the time between image captures (in seconds)

<br/>

7. **Question 7** A fixed-wing drone flies at a constant speed of 12 m/s. The image height on the ground (in the flight direction) is 60 meters. What should the **photo interval (seconds per image)** be to maintain at least 67% front overlap? Use the same equation as above.

<br/>

8. **Question 8** Your drone camera has a ground image width of 120 meters at the planned altitude. You are targeting 75% lateral overlap for 3D reconstruction of terrain. How far apart should your **parallel flight lines** (flight line spacing) be? Use the equation below.


$$
\text{Lateral Overlap (%)} = \left( \frac{\text{Photo Width} - \text{Row Spacing}}{\text{Photo Width}} \right) \times 100
$$

- *Photo Width* is the ground coverage width of each image (in meters)
- *Row Spacing* is the distance between adjacent flight lines (in meters)

<br/>

9. **Question 9** You are using a drone camera with the following specs: Sensor width of 13.2 mm, image width of 4000 pixels, and focal length of 8.8 mm. You want to fly at an altitude that gives you a GSD of 2.5 cm/pixel. Estimate the **altitude (in meters)** required to achieve this GSD. GSD can also be calculated with the following equation. *Pay attention to units.*


$$
GSD = \frac{\text{Sensor Width (m)} \times H (masl)}{\text{Focal Length (m)} \times \text{Image Width (pixels)}}
$$

- *H* is the flight altitude in meters


<br/>

10. **Question 10** At 90 meters AGL, your drone’s image footprint on the ground has a Width of 120 meters and Height of 80 meters. You are mapping an area 500 meters long (in the direction of flight) and 300 meters wide (across flight lines). You want 70% front overlap and 65% lateral overlap. How many **images** (total number) are needed to image this site? Use equations and information below to answer.

As a crude estimation, the distance length (L) or width (W) (in meters) can be used along with the overlap distance to estimate the number of images required:

$$
\text{Number of images} = \lceil \frac{Area~Length~(or~Width)}{\text{Spacing}} \rceil
$$
The spacing relates to the equation in question five. For simplistic area estimations, you can multiply length and width based on the dimensions of your study area.

However, a much better estimation would consider the actual image footprint on the ground in relation to the full area and include the first image rather than only spacing to estimate number of images. 

Instead, use the following equation to better estimate the total image count. 

$$
\text{Number of Images}_{\text{direction 1}} = \left\lceil \frac{\text{Area Length} - \text{Image Length}}{\text{ Spacing}} \right\rceil + 1
$$
Again, spacing relates to the equations in question 5.
